en: They dismounted and ran,
Striding awkwardly;
Akkelte and Kökchybuk—
They readied them and took them in hand.
Chinese flint and liver-stone
The heroes struck together,
And set fire to their matchcords.
The purest of marksmen,
His forked gun-rest stood ready.
When they reached the pass,
Let me tell of the hero's state:
Semetey now prepared to shoot,
And your uncle Bakai then
Implored Semetey:
“Oh, my river spring in a valley,
My champion, gained at death’s door!
Oh, my pale-gray, solemn darling,
My gray hawk, my morning star!
Before now you had not reconnoitered the road to Beijing,
Gone out on the hunt and shot a wild ram,
Nor gained practice with wild game!
You had not judged the quarry’s course,
Nor, standing forth in triumph,
Had you shot down Akkulja!
My beloved foal,
Do not stare too high by accident,
Or loose your aim awry;
Do not let your bullet fly too far,
Lest Kuukulja escape alive
And bring about our ruin!
Let it not dig my deep grave,
Carry this news to its khan,
And set my sorrow boiling!
Let it not give news to the army,
Give the news to its khan,
So that all the Chinese converge,
Drawing their bows like rain,
Firing bullets like hail,
And amid the dense dust,
Standing their ground to fight,
Leave us caught in blackest night.
Give this orphaned soul your support;
The knack of Akkelte was mine,
My breast was wise and my hand skilled,
I had the needed mastery;
When I went hunting I was fortunate,
And had the finest skill!
You who once knew no failure
Had a champion’s prowess;
Do not overshoot,
You careless, headstrong child!
While Bakai spoke in this way,
Fierce anger seized him;
At his uncle, old Bakai,
The blood-drinking one raged
As though he would swallow him whole:
“You have a chest, but no eyes;
Buried old uncle, what are you saying?!
Your beard is white as a swan,
And when the journey is close at hand,
You rush about saying, ‘I shall shoot’—
Time-stricken uncle, what are you saying?!
Long ago, when you were young,
You grew used to shooting wild rams;
You do not recognize your own decrepitude,
You worn-out champion, old man,
And will not stop contesting the road!”
Semetey grew furious,
Gripped Akkelte and pulled it to him;
When Bakai grappled for it,
He swept him aside with his left hand.
Ah, withered world, be damned—
Your aged uncle Bakai
He shoved away, leaving him standing gaunt.
Today the death of your uncle Bakai
At last became plain.
“Bakai was once a great khan;
Take me now without further torment,”
Bakai said, sitting hunched.
“I was once a great man;
God, take me before I suffer this,”
Bakai said, sitting hunched.
Your uncle, once mountain-like,
Stooped like a camel sunk to its knees.
Kuukulja, watching from its lookout,
Set off at a rolling run,
Struck a black rock as large as a house
With a resounding crash;
First butting against a stone
Was the wild ram’s habit,
Then it would tear off grass.
Kuukulja made straight ahead,
Parting like blue mist,
Beneath your gray wolf,
Showing half a target.
When the wild ram appeared,
Akkelte, left by Manas,
He bent into position and took aim;
With a thunderous bang, at the ram,
At the accursed creature’s flank,
He sent the shot flying.
The excited braggart
Raised his gaze and watched;
From a spear’s length away, the wild ram
He had shot at long range.
Then your uncle Bakai
Tore at his beard and flung it,
Tugged at his mustache and cast it aside.
When placed in front, he was good fortune;
When following behind, he was like a countless army.
He found words in sudden peril,
And found sight in darkness.
Your uncle, old Bakai,
Was the holy sage left behind
By bloodthirsty lion Manas.
Do not ask how your uncle fared:
Your uncle Bakai roared,
Stamping the ground beneath him,
And scolded his young Semetey:
“Alas, swollen fool, be damned;
May there never be two such as you!
Did I not tell you earlier?
Did you not hear me earlier?
By shooting the wild ram from afar,
Have you set my sorrow boiling?”
In fury he scolded him,
And Bakai charged at him;
His bloodthirsty hero’s Akkelte
He tore now from his hand.
Fine-grained powder for rapid fire—
The careful, hapless Bakai
Readied it in his slender hand,
And poured the powder with a rattle.
He struck the gunstock once against the ground;
Your uncle, lion Bakai,
Held the gun firm as a bullet
And leveled it at Akkulja.
As it was about to cross
The rise shaped like a saddleback,
Your uncle Bakai, the keen hunter,
Judged the moment with cunning.
A tremendous commotion
Akkelte unleashed as it fired;
Straight through Akkulja’s waist
Akkelte’s shot passed!
Akkelte cracked aloud,
And the wild ram fell with a thud!
Having shot down the wild ram,
Gray-wolf elder Bakai
Had a thousand cares within his breast,
And tears enough for a thousand plains!
He struck his chest with a crack,
His heart torn apart;
From your uncle, old Bakai,
The tears poured down!
Smoke billowed from his mouth,
And tears streamed from his eyes.
“Alas, Manas, would that you had not died;
Would that Bakai had not lived to see this disgrace!
When I besieged Kara-Shaar and Kambyl,
When I held them under siege,
When I made the Manchus howl
And beat them down,
Why did I not die then!
When I wore at a jaunty tilt
My double-lapelled sable cap,
When I mounted Beijing’s throne
And lived in delight,
Why did I not die then!
When I disdained the whole world,
While my mighty Manas lived,
I had not lived to see such a thing;
My eyes reddening like a raven’s,
This wretched soul of mine until now
Had somehow gone on without dying!
My horns broken, left blunt,
I have become hornless!
Bereft of mane and tail,
I have become a mere stump!
Alas, Manas, damn you for dying;
Would that Bakai had not lived to see disgrace!
My sire died—what a day of sorrow—
And a camel’s load was laid upon a yearling;
When my lord passed from sight,
I herded camels to survive—
Why was I cast into such hell!
Failing to die beside my companion,
I have lived on in ruin;
Parted from my comrade,
Out on the empty steppe
I have been left to howl!
When I fitted a head
To the black spear Zulpukor,
While leopard Manas lived,
When infidel and Muslim alike
I led at the head,
Why did I not die then!
When I swung the curved blade
Against my forearm,
When I shattered
And took the face of the earth,
In the full strength of my courage,
While my bloodthirsty hero lived,
Why did I not die then!
When I hung a battle-axe
Upon the lattice wall,
When Manas had need of me,
At the earth’s edge, Zhelpinish,
When I knew that land,
Why did I not die then!
I did not suffer the grave’s torment;
Beneath my gray wolf
I did not die as a sacrifice!
When he rode out to battle,
Loading bullets upon the elephant,
Gathering the Muslim people together,
Driving the people in surging ranks,
Massing the giants in firm array,
Leading all the Muslim nation,
When he brought his wrath upon Kakan,
When he battered
The Black Chinese Manchus,
And seized their khanate,
Why did I not die then!
When my anger made blood flow,
When I held them under siege,
When I beat down the strong men
Of the coat-wearing Chinese,
When I thrashed them,
Why did I not die then!
Alas, Manas, damn you for dying!
I was left behind in disgrace;
Do not let Bakai be overcome—
My lion Manas, take me with you!
Companion of the other world,
Did you cast me behind you
To be shoved about by everyone,
And leave me to be slaughtered like this?!
You were a leopard-born warrior;
Manas of the dark day, damn you for dying!
While Manas lived,
I would carve the elephant’s flesh and eat it;
Pride had carried me away,
And I would say, ‘Let calamity remain far off!’
While Manas lived,
I was a great man, I was a khan;
To every people who saw me, I, Bakai,
Was a man like a prophet.
My lion Manas, have you truly gone,
When Bakai had grown old,
Did you leave him behind?!"
Leaning his golden-cheeked battle-axe
Against his right side,
Bakai stood there wailing!
Mourning Manas then
Remembering the past
